author: UpwindMDR
text:
🚨 HIGH - Two Unauthenticated Denial-of-Service Flaws in vLLM Inference Engine (CVE-2026-130685 & CVE-2026-130686)

The vLLM project has released version 0.33.0 addressing two high-severity, unauthenticated remote Denial-of-Service (DoS) vulnerabilities affecting LLM inference deployments:

• CVE-2026-130685: Improper input validation when served with --skip-tokenizer-init allows attackers to submit out-of-range prompt token IDs to /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings, or /pooling - bypassing vocab checks and crashing the shared EngineCore across all tenants.
• CVE-2026-130686: Missing request-wide media budgets allow attackers to submit numerous remote image URLs in a single compact request to /v1/messages or /v1/responses, forcing image downloads/decoding before prompt-length checks and exhausting memory, CPU, and connections.

👉 Affected / Remediation: Affects vLLM 0.28.0 prior to 0.33.0 (CVE-2026-130685) and 0.6.0 prior to 0.33.0 (CVE-2026-130686). Upgrade immediately to vLLM 0.33.0 or later, and avoid exposing vLLM APIs directly to untrusted networks without authentication and rate limiting.

author: AzmyBlog
text:
Gave your AI agent or BI tool a "read-only" Postgres user and called it safe?

That user can run code on your database server.

CVE-2026-116331: a plain login role can do it. Postgres gives every role TEMPORARY on the database by default, and that's enough. No access to your tables needed.

Same researcher did it on MySQL and ClickHouse too.

Grants protect your data. They don't protect the engine.

Upgrade to 18.7 / 17.12 / 16.16 / 15.20 / 14.25 and run REVOKE TEMPORARY ON DATABASE ... FROM PUBLIC.

https://t.co/aNcPO6jEo7

author: Ldataengineer
text:
𝗔 𝗣𝗼𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁 𝗣𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗪𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗢𝘂𝘁 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁'𝘀 𝗢𝘄𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲
Two days ago, Microsoft's 𝚊𝚐𝚎𝚗𝚝-𝚏𝚛𝚊𝚖𝚎𝚠𝚘𝚛𝚔 package on PyPI shipped a credential stealer. It gets about 𝟰𝟭,𝟬𝟬𝟬 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱𝘀 𝗮 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸.

Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 went up on 17 Nov, 33 minutes apart, and both were gone within the hour.

The malware isn't the worrying part. Wiz says 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗱 𝗮 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗘𝗦𝗥𝗣, the internal service Microsoft uses to sign and publish the package. An upload from AWS got blocked by IP filtering. One from Microsoft-owned IP space went straight through. Nobody knows yet how they got the certificate.

The stealer sat in a .𝚙𝚝𝚑 file, so it ran whenever Python started. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗮𝗴𝗲. It went after Azure tokens, CI secrets, and npm, pip, git and Docker credentials.

There's an AI twist too. The tooling calls itself Cairn, an open-source AI pentest framework, and Wiz says the attacker's own test run caught what looks like a Pi coding agent on a GLM model.

So far the damage is small: Wiz counts 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘃𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗺𝘀. If you use the package, pin 1.26.0, look for both .𝚙𝚝𝚑 files, and rotate anything that environment could see.

𝗔 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗿, 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲, 𝗶𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁. 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗶𝗻.

If you use it:

• 𝗣𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝟭.𝟮𝟲.𝟬, the last clean release, and search lockfiles and images for 1.26.1 and 1.26.2
• 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵 .𝗽𝘁𝗵 𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘀. Searching for the 1.26.1 file alone misses 1.26.2
• 𝗥𝗼𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗲. Stolen managed-identity and OIDC tokens last up to 24 hours
